overview: This file documents the disappearance and discovery of a Japan Air Transport Company passenger aircraft, the Envoy (DAOL), during a flight from Giran to Taihoku in northern Taiwan on March 7, 1940. American Consul Gerald Warner first reported the missing aircraft, its eight occupants—including German mechanical engineer Enno Topp—and the weather-hampered search, while emphasizing that no Americans were aboard. A subsequent despatch reported that the wreckage had been found on Qixing Mountain and that everyone aboard had died; the papers also discuss previous regional air accidents and proposed improvements to radio, weather-reporting, telephone, and routing arrangements. The bundle includes the initial despatch, a confirmation copy of Warner’s telegram to Tokyo, the follow-up despatch, and a map enclosure locating the crash.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 97 on the disappearance of the Envoy
subfiles.about: Reports the disappearance of a Japan Air Transport Company passenger aircraft between Giran and Taihoku and confirms that no Americans were aboard.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports that the Envoy (DAOL) disappeared in bad weather on March 7 with a pilot, mechanic, six passengers, and no radio equipment. The passengers included Police Officer Imai and his daughter, other Japanese travelers, and German mechanical engineer Enno Topp, whose family was to be notified through Japanese authorities in Shanghai. About 6,000 police and Young Men’s Society members were searching the mountains, while aviation authorities considered radios, improved weather reporting, dedicated airport telephone service, and use of the longer sea route. Warner also places the incident in the context of earlier fatal accidents near the Penghu and at Giran, as well as accidents near the Ryukyu Islands.

subfiles.title: Confirmation copy of Warner’s telegram to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Briefly alerts the Tokyo consulate to the missing aircraft, its passengers, the unsuccessful search, and the absence of American casualties.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that the Envoy disappeared on the short Giran-to-Taihoku flight with a pilot, mechanic, three Japanese adults, two Japanese children, and German engineer Enno Topp. It notes that fog was obstructing a widespread search and explicitly says that no Americans were aboard. Unexplained text at the foot of the page reads “Foreign Intercourse,” names “Corall Miller,” and gives the date March 2, 1942.

subfiles.title: Despatch reporting discovery of the Envoy wreckage
subfiles.about: Reports that the missing Envoy had been found wrecked on Qixing Mountain and that all eight occupants were killed.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports that the completely demolished aircraft was found about half a mile below the summit of Qixing Mountain in the Datun range. He suggests that the pilot may have abandoned an attempted mountain crossing and tried to follow the coast, but visibility was so poor that ships could not enter Keelung harbor. The wreckage was located from the air on the first clear morning after the disappearance, and the scattered debris indicated that all eight occupants died instantly. The Taiwan Government-General assumed responsibility for the German passenger’s body and effects, while families, police, and the airline handled the Japanese victims’ remains.

subfiles.title: Map showing the site of the Envoy crash
subfiles.about: Locates the March 7, 1940 crash of the Envoy on the side of Qixing Mountain.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure is a map of Taiwan marking the crash site, captioned with the date and the deaths of all six passengers, the pilot, and the mechanic. The mountain’s name is rendered “Shiohiseizan” in the caption, evidently a variant or OCR corruption of “Shichiseizan.”

interest: The file provides a compact case study of civil aviation hazards in colonial Taiwan, combining a real-time missing-aircraft report with the later identification of the crash site. Its detailed reconstruction of the aircraft’s sightings and route, the composition of the search force, and proposed safety reforms is especially useful for studying navigation, communications, and emergency response before routine airborne radio equipment. The treatment of Enno Topp also illustrates the consular complications surrounding a foreign victim in a territory without German representation, while the map preserves a precise contemporary representation of the crash location.
